paras: The shooting of Ed Gardner took place in the jail at Murray, Kentucky, on Monday, July 7, 1919, when a Black prisoner was shot in the leg during an argument with jailer Albert James and his guards. Gardner, who had been held on a whiskey-selling charge, then faced a charge of assault, according to a brief dispatch printed in the Dallas Express.
Gardner, described as "a Negro prisoner," had been jailed at Murray on a charge of selling whiskey.

When James entered the jail on Monday, he ordered Gardner to "get off that cot" and to take food into another part of the jail. Gardner did not move quickly enough to suit the jailer, and an argument followed in which guards were involved. During the argument Gardner was shot in the leg with a revolver; the printed text is garbled at this point and leaves unclear whether a guard or the jailer fired.

A charge of assault was afterward preferred, apparently against Gardner himself. The coverage does not report how badly Gardner was hurt, the outcome of the charges against him, or any action against the officers.

The only report found ran on the front page of the Dallas Express on July 12, 1919, under a Murray dateline of July 10. It carried no headline of its own and was printed without comment at the foot of an unrelated article about the Rand School losing its charter. The dispatch gave the jailer's words and the sequence of the argument in a flat, matter-of-fact register, identifying Gardner by race but stating no motive beyond his slowness in obeying.
